up-28.claim: The Reporters' Collective reported that it compared the Commission's data for 55 of Pilibhit's 419 booths with the final roll of 10 April 2026, matching entries by EPIC number, and found 2,691 entries in which the elector's name and the relative's name had been replaced by different names, 5.7 per cent of the electors at those booths. It said 2,372 of the changes were made in August, 656 of them on 19 August within 7.4 minutes between 6.26 pm and 6.34 pm, and that 523 were made on 31 August within 19.4 minutes. It said the Urdu roll still carried the original details where the English and Hindi rolls had been changed. It checked 15 of the cases on the ground against two government photo identity documents for each and found that the documents matched the original entries in the final roll. When it checked again eight days after the Chief Electoral Officer's finding of 22 October, 2,638 of the 2,691 changed entries were still on the roll. Two booth level officers told it that the tehsil office asked them to verify a set of Form 8 applications and then told them, before they began, that the applications had already been resolved.

up-33.headline: UP could add over 1 crore voters through electoral roll revision
up-33.claim: The Times of India reported on 5 November that the rural panchayat rolls in Uttar Pradesh, finalised on 10 June 2026, hold 12.58 crore electors and the urban local body rolls, published on 2 April 2023, hold 4.33 crore, 16.91 crore in all, against 13.46 crore electors on the Assembly rolls on 7 October 2026, a difference of nearly 3.45 crore. The Chief Electoral Officer, Navdeep Rinwa, told the paper that the Assembly rolls hold about 10.20 crore rural electors, about 2.38 crore fewer than the 12.58 crore on the panchayat rolls. The paper puts the urban electors on the Assembly rolls at about 3.36 crore, nearly 97 lakh fewer than the urban local body rolls hold. Rinwa said the panchayat rolls were revised with 1 January 2026 as the qualifying date, while the Assembly rolls also take in people who turn 18 on 1 April, 1 July and 1 October. He said the special summary revision could add more than one crore electors to the roll. He cited a district-level verification carried out after court proceedings involving the two election authorities, which found 144 eligible people missing from the Assembly roll once dead, duplicate, shifted and untraceable electors were excluded, about 7% of the entries examined. The paper says those findings led to the order to compare the Assembly rolls with the panchayat and urban local body rolls across the state (up-32). By the paper's figures the Assembly rolls held 15.4 crore electors before the Special Intensive Revision and 13.39 crore when it ended on 10 April 2026.
up-33.quote: There is a clear difference between the two lists. This is despite the fact that assembly electoral rolls have four qualifying dates, whereas panchayat rolls have only one.
up-33.response: Rinwa told the paper that the comparison is not exact, because the municipal rolls were last revised in 2023 and the Assembly rolls are current, and that the differences cannot be taken as eligible people who are not registered, because the rolls may hold dead electors, people who have moved, duplicate entries and other ineligible names. The rural and urban figures as reported, 10.20 and 3.36 crore, make 13.56 crore, 10 lakh more than the 13.46 crore total, and the paper does not explain the difference. The Free Press Journal reports that the State Election Commission prepares the panchayat rolls and the Election Commission of India the Assembly and Lok Sabha rolls, and puts the difference between the panchayat rolls and the rural electors on the Assembly rolls at nearly 2.4 crore.

up-40.claim: The Chief Electoral Officer of Uttar Pradesh, Navdeep Rinwa, directed District Election Officers on Saturday, 14 November, to fix responsibility for serious errors in the roll during the special summary revision for 2027, The Times of India reported on 15 November. Booth level officers found responsible between 17 November and 16 December for errors in names, ages, gender or addresses, or for duplicate entries, may lose up to one month's honorarium, according to the number and seriousness of the errors. Their supervisors may lose up to a month's honorarium where poor supervision leaves members of one household at different polling stations or in different sections of the roll. Electoral registration officers and assistant electoral registration officers are to be assessed from 7 November, when the roll was frozen, to 4 January 2027, when the final roll is due, and serious lapses in scrutiny, supervision or the disposal of applications may bring deductions from their honorarium in proportion, for that period of nearly two months. Dainik Jagran puts the deduction for them at up to about two months' honorarium, for lapses that include the acceptance or rejection of claims and objections. Booth level officers are to scrutinise the roll of their polling stations at their desks from 17 to 20 November and correct errors in names, photographs, ages, gender and addresses through Form 8 applications from the electors concerned. The draft roll is to be published on 17 November and claims and objections taken until 16 December, with special camps at all 1,73,730 polling stations on 21, 22, 28 and 29 November, when booth level officers are to be present from 10 am to 4 pm.
